extracted.intended_audience: university educators, administrators, and students interested in the philosophy and aims of higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles and standards for what counts as a proper university education (liberal vs. professional/utility-focused), including pedagogy (residence, tutorials), curriculum breadth vs depth, and the intellectual aims of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal education defined as cultivation of the intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberal Education is the training of the intellect to apprehend and contemplate truth; its cultivation lies in fitting the mind to apprehend truth rather than in immediate practical or professional ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an acquired faculty of judgment, clear-sightedness, sagacity, philosophical reach, and intellectual self-possession that results from discipline and habit; it is not mere acquisition of facts or passive reception of details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education must require exertion, grounding, and progressive advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is not to be 'without exertion, without attention, without toil; without grounding, without advance, without finishing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: the belief that printing presses, lectures, or mere multiplication of volumes will passively enlighten minds; relying on passive dissemination rather than disciplined study undermines true education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth over superficial breadth (avoid smattering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A smattering in many branches (superficial acquaintance with chemistry, geology, astronomy, political economy, etc.) is not enlargement but shallowness; 'a thorough knowledge of one science and a superficial acquaintance with many, are not the same thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: avoid forcing students to learn many subjects badly; prefer mastery of individual subjects. Anti-patterns: curricula that load memory with undigested knowledge or encourage 'learning all at once' rather than sequential, well-grounded study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recreations and accomplishments are not education
rubrics_metrics.description: Accomplishments and innocent recreations (drawing, fencing, botany, conchology, specimen-collecting, membership of institutions) may be graceful or useful leisure but do not 'form or cultivate the intellect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call things by their right names: amusements that refresh or keep one from vice are valuable but should not be conflated with education. Avoid substituting elegant pastimes for intellectual training.

rubrics_metrics.name: University as Alma Mater: personal, resident, tutorial supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: A University should be an Alma Mater that knows its children one by one (residence and tutorial superintendence), not merely an examining-foundry that awards degrees to external candidates who pass wide-ranging exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer residence and tutorial oversight to impersonal examination-only systems. The college community, mutual sympathy, and personal knowledge of students produce genuine discipline of intellect; anti-patterns include universities that dispense degrees without personal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of collegiate community and self-education through association
rubrics_metrics.description: When young men come together and freely mix, they learn from one another; conversation and the community act as a series of lectures, producing self-education, common standards, and a 'genius loci' or tradition that molds individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize shared intellectual atmosphere, mutual influence, and the self-perpetuating tradition of a college as central pedagogical goods; solitary or purely exam-driven education lacks this benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer self-education to ineffective formal teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-education (properly understood) is preferable to a system of teaching that professes much yet does little for the mind; independent, thoughtful study may yield more genuine enlargement than formal but shallow instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveats: purely self-taught individuals may lack common grounding and risk eccentricity or gaps; many learners still need stimulus and instructor support. The standard favors systems that truly cultivate thought rather than produce mere application to exams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training is a matter of rule, not mere application or accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual training requires systematic rules and discipline; merely reading many books, attending lectures, or witnessing experiments falls short of forming the mental powers needed to discern truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal is development of faculties to compare, combine, correct, and build up ideas; curriculum and pedagogy should be designed to cultivate these operations rather than to maximize exposure alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should form powers of discrimination and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Education must give the power to discriminate between truth and falsehood, to sift grains of truth from the mass, to arrange things by real value, and to advance beyond acquired knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess educational success by students' abilities in judgment, sagacity, self-possession, and to 'push things up to their first principles,' not merely by memorized content or rhetorical polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate utility narrowly with educational value
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of making 'Utility' the sole measure of education: useful for a profession is not the only or highest end; a liberal education is 'good in itself' and therefore also broadly useful in diffusing good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two senses of utility: (a) narrow professional usefulness for an individual's trade, and (b) the broader instrumental utility of promoting good. A university can be 'useful' by cultivating intellect even if not vocationally training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum choice should be guided by whether studies cultivate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to teach classics, sciences, or other subjects should depend on whether those studies 'tend to mental culture'—i.e., whether they cultivate the understanding, habits of original inquiry, and the habit of pushing things to first principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dogmatic curriculum choices; prioritize studies that form 'the understanding' and habits of rigorous thought. The evaluation criterion is mental culture rather than prestige or perceived dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to mechanistic, exam-driven, multi-subject testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that exact of students 'an acquaintance with every science under the sun' by examinations, forcing them to 'load their minds with a score of subjects against an examination,' produce application without true understanding and often lead to later abandonment of learned material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assessment and degree requirements to favor depth and intellectual formation. Anti-patterns: intermittent exams in many unrelated subjects, impersonal examiners, or curricula connected by 'no wide philosophy.'
